newsitem.title: UK: FTSE 100 sinks to day's lows despite in-line CPI.
newsitem.headline: FTSE 100 sinks to day's lows despite in-line CPI.

text.p: UK's leading FTSE 100 shed more than 1.4 percent early in the afternoon session on Monday as concerns about the contents of the UK budget overwhelmed investors.
The blue chip index was down 72.2 points to 4,672.9 by 1305 GMT, shrugging off in-line U.S. inflation data that was expected to to spur a higher start on Wall Street.
"There's probably value out there...but who is going to buy ahead of the budget, with the looming threat of a cut to the dividend tax credit," one dealer said.
UK shares tracked a FTSE futures and gilts lower, ignoring news that U.S. consumer prices had risen by just 0.1 percent in May, compared with a market consensus of a 0.2 percent increase.
U.S. blue chips were forecast to open steady to higher, buoyed by the belief that the Federal Reserve won't raise interest rates at its next policy meeting on July 2.
"The (U.S. inflation) figures are all pointing to the fact that inflation in the U.S. economy is dead," Yamaichi international bond strategist Adam Chester told Reuters Financial Television.

Sentiment was knocked at the beginning of the week on rumours the Treasury could abolish a current tax break allowing pension funds to reclaim advance corporation tax paid by companies on their dividends.
"It looks like the tax credit will go," said another trader. "It's just too tempting a target for the government to resist, and if it does, the market should go down quite a bit further."

Uncertainty surrounding the Budget is likely to keep investors wary for the next few weeks, traders said. "We are going to have Budget blues," another added. "There's just no reason to buy this market."
Lehman Brothers UK stock strategist Ian Scott has maintained his overweight recommendation and his year-end target of 5,000 for the FTSE 100.
He believes on an earnings basis, UK equities remain cheap relative to both gilts and other global equity markets.
Scott said Monday's reaction to the Budget story "suggests that reform of the existing arrangements has, in large part, already been priced into the equity market."

"Nevertheless, there is probably still some further modest downside for the market should ACT (Advanced Corporate Tax) credits be completely abolished with no offsetting corporate tax cuts elsewhere," he added.

Among individual stocks, shares in British Sky Broadcasting Group Plc dropped 21-1/2p to 566-1/2p after the company said chief executive Sam Chisolm was to step down at the end of the year on medical advice.
Shares in Imperial Chemical Industries Plc tumbled 27p to 822 as profit-taking ended a recent sprint upwards, analysts said.
ICI had been one of the best performing FTSE 100 stocks after the chemicals group on May 7 announced it would buy Unilever's speciality chemicals business.
Shares in Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc rose on Tuesday after Goldman Sachs added the two companies to its "recommended" list.
Grand Met was up 9-1/2p at 575p while Guinness added 2-1/2p to 582-1/2.
The U.S. investment bank set a price target of 662p for both companies', which are in the process of merging.
